meaning: 'The Fish' — the first avatāra of Viṣṇu, who saved Manu and the Vedas from the great deluge

phonemes.desc: Short a as in “cup”; the word is the common noun “fish”.
The cluster tsy is pronounced “chya” in the north, “tsya” in the south: MAT-chyuh.
The first avatāra of Vishnu — the fish that saved Manu from the flood.

kin.label: Lineage
kin.form: first of the daśāvatāra, the ten descents

pronunciation.note: The flood-saviour as fish: the oldest of Vishnu’s descents, and the closest of India’s myths to the world’s other flood-legends.

domains.title: The Fish, First Avatāra of Viṣṇu
domains.subtitle: The Flood-Saviour of Manu
domains.lead: Matsya is Vishnu’s first descent: the great fish that warned Manu of the coming flood, bade him build a ship, and bore it — and with it the seven sages, the seeds of every species, and the Vedas themselves — through the drowning of the world to the one un-submerged peak. The Purāṇic telling makes him the keeper of the scriptures as well as the race.

cards.name: The Great Fish
cards.desc: A tiny fish that outgrew every vessel, until only the ocean could hold it — Vishnu himself.

cards.name: The Deluge
cards.desc: The pralaya, the world’s dissolution by water — the flood that ends each cycle of creation.

cards.name: The Ship of Manu
cards.desc: The ark of Hindu myth: the seven sages and the seeds of all life aboard, tied to the fish’s horn.

cards.name: Keeper of the Vedas
cards.desc: The demon Hayagrīva stole the scriptures; the fish slew him and returned the Vedas to the world.

mythology.lead: The Matsya myth is India’s flood-saga: the warning, the ark, the world’s drowning, and the mooring at the one remaining peak — with the added theology of the avatāra, Vishnu descending to preserve both species and scripture. The telling grows from a brief Vedic episode to one of the Purāṇas’ most beloved complete narratives.

myths.title: The Earliest Flood
myths.text: The oldest telling is dry and swift: Manu finds a tiny fish, rears it through successively larger vessels until only the sea will hold it; it warns him of the coming flood and returns as a horned leviathan to tow his ship by a cable. At the flood’s peak they moor on the one un-submerged tree — the nyagrodha — and the fish reveals itself as ‘the lord of creatures’.

myths.title: The Full Narrative
myths.text: The eponymous Purāṇa expands everything: the demon Hayagrīva steals the four Vedas as Brahmā sleeps; Vishnu wakes as a fish, kills Hayagrīva in the world-river’s depths, and returns the scriptures; then the flood proper — the ark, the sages, the seeds, and the long tow to the Himalayan peak where the new world begins.

myths.title: The First Descent
myths.text: In the daśāvatāra sequence, Matsya is the first: preservation precedes power. The theology reads each avatāra as the god’s answer to a cosmic emergency — here, the emergency is knowledge itself, the Vedas drowned or stolen. The fish saves the texts before it saves the species.

myths.title: One Deluge, Many Arks
myths.text: The flood-list is the world’s most widespread myth-complex: Utnapishtim in the Gilgamesh epic, Noah in Genesis, Deucalion in Greece, and Manu in the Purāṇas. The Indian telling’s distinctive signature is the warning fish — the saviour who speaks, and the god who tows.

lore.syncretism: Matsya is the Purāṇic systematization of a Vedic flood-episode — the Brahmana’s ‘lord of creatures’ identified with Vishnu when the avatāra-doctrine matured. Comparative mythology groups him with the ancient Near Eastern flood-saviours; and in the daśāvatāra art of Southeast Asia, he rides the temple walls as the sequence’s first figure.
lore.culturalLegacy: The Matsya Jayanti festival celebrates his descent; and the flood-narrative is every Indian schoolchild’s introduction to comparative mythology. The story’s signature image — the fish that outgrows every vessel — became a parable of the infinite in domestic teaching: the god who cannot be kept in any pot.
lore.extendedMeditation: Matsya: the fish that saved the words. Restored plainly, the name is the simplest in the avatāra sequence — the common noun for the creature that carried scripture and species through the drowning of the world. Two syllables, one ark, all the Vedas.
lore.archaeology: Matsya rides the first panel of every daśāvatāra frieze — from the Gupta reliefs of Deogarh to the great sequence-walls of Angkor. The fish-torso Vishnu of the early medieval images is his monumental form.
lore.cult: The Matsya Jayanti festival (spring) celebrates the descent; and the jalayātrā boat-festivals of riverine India echo the ark-myth in their liturgy. His temples are rare, but his image opens every ten-incarnation cycle.
lore.iconography: Fish-torso and god-head, the horn projecting from his snout for the ship’s cable; or the great fish alone bearing the ark on its back. His emblem is the horn — the hitch-point of salvation.
lore.reception: Comparative mythology’s flood-paradigm uses Matsya as the eastern anchor of the deluge-complex — the same story told from the Indus to the Jordan. The avatar-doctrine’s scholars cite him as the clearest case of a myth upgraded into a theology: the old fish, re-signed as the first descent.
